subject: 3BE6E42E9BA44C61A8C86EA2B6F82BEA
introduction: “The thirsty one must run after the water; the fountain will not run after those who are thirsty.” The guide gathers what the Bahá’í writings say about the seeker’s part: patience, thirst, fairness, detachment from inherited opinion, unresting effort, and a refusal ever to be satisfied; and it sets beside these the assurances that no sincere seeker is turned away. Jesus’s “seek, and ye shall find” is quoted in the guide itself, and Jeremiah, Proverbs and the parables of the pearl, the treasure and the lost coin say the same. Bacon, Kant and the Bereans stand for the fair-minded inquirer, Browning and Tennyson for the unsatisfied one, Sa‘dí’s moth for the lover. Three voices turn the picture round: Thompson’s Hound of Heaven, in which God does the pursuing; the one who stands at the door and knocks; and Paul’s “not of him that runneth”. Pascal’s “thou wouldst not seek me, if thou hadst not found me” holds both.
questions: The readings name several conditions of search. Which do you find hardest: patience, fairness, detachment or perseverance?
“The fountain will not run after those who are thirsty”, yet readings 34 to 36 promise that the seeker is met. Put the two together. What does Thompson’s poem add?
Reading 14 says there is nothing worse than satisfaction. What is the difference between the peace of having found and the complacency being warned against?
The Buddha’s man with the arrow wanted every question answered first. What does a seeker need to know before acting?
Reading 5 asks for detachment from all one has heard. Is such fair-mindedness possible, and how would one practise it?

outside.why: “The steed of this valley is patience.” Let us run with patience the race that is set before us.
The husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it.
The fountain is gushing, but there must be thirst. Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters.
As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.

“The fountain will not run after those who are thirsty.” Francis Thompson’s poem says it does: I fled Him, down the nights and down the days, and was pursued. Which matches your experience, and can both be true?

Some stand at the garden gate and do not care to enter. Here it is the other who stands outside: behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in. Who is waiting for whom?
First, fair-mindedness and detachment. Bacon’s rule for a reader: read not to contradict and confute, nor to believe and take for granted, but to weigh and consider.
The Bereans received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
The seeker enters the Garden of Search. Ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.
If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures; then shalt thou find the knowledge of God.
The searching itself: she lights a candle, and sweeps the house, and seeks diligently till she find it.
Search, and be enraptured with whatever holy soul has the truth. A merchant man, seeking goodly pearls, who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had.
The lamp of search, striving, longing, love and rapture. By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not. I will rise now, and seek him.
Augustine’s sentence for the same longing: You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You.
Immerse yourselves in the ocean of My words. Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
It is incumbent to be a seeker after every truth. Aristotle: all men by nature desire to know.
Kant’s motto for an age of inquiry: Sapere aude! Have courage to use your own reason!
Strive night and day. As for those who strive in Us, We surely guide them to Our paths.

“The first thing to do is to acquire …”, said with a serious face. The Buddha warned of a search that never starts: a man shot with a poisoned arrow who will not have it removed until he knows who shot it. What questions can a seeker safely leave unanswered?
Come to the spiritual table hungry. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
“Man must never get satisfied.” Browning: a man’s reach should exceed his grasp, or what’s a Heaven for?
The satisfied church: because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
Let the flame of search burn fiercely. Tennyson’s Ulysses, old: strong in will to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
Only one willing to be a moth around the flame will shine. Sa‘dí: learn love from the moth, because it burnt, lost its life, and found no voice.
Every expenditure needs an income. Which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?
Refine the eye of the heart to distinguish truth from falsehood. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Rest not; free yourselves. Forgetting those things which are behind, I press toward the mark.
The search for truth is a heavy burden. Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
Verses recited to a stone for a thousand years would not move it. Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth.
If you thirst, the waves are near. Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst.
When the desire for knowledge reaches its height, a teacher is sent. Philip was sent to a road in the desert, to a man reading: understandest thou what thou readest?
Thou disappointest not him that hath sought Thee. The Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him.
No one who seeks will be disappointed. If he comes to Me walking, I go to him running.
All creation speaks of God but seeks Him not. That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us.
The Revelation as an ocean with pearls in its depths. The kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field.
The soul whose search is real leaves nothing undone. Pascal hears: thou wouldst not seek me, if thou hadst not found me. Is the seeker’s effort the cause of finding or its first sign?

Paul on the other side: it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. How do the readings combine the demand for effort with the promise of grace (see 34 to 36)?
The reading is this saying: ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
The best teacher is an ordinary believer who has consecrated himself. Not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, are called.

shortfall: Readings 16, 18 to 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 31, 32, 38, 39 and 41 exhort to effort or greet a seeker in terms already given companions.
